originalTitle: Tesla is inviting some people to buy a Cybercab ‘for personal use’ — but read the fine print
summary: Tesla is doubling, or perhaps tripling down on its bold claims of an autonomous future with the offer to "select customers" to purchase a Cybercab for "personal use." But the gilded, steering-wheel-free two-seater will "only be available in supported service areas" - meaning you'll only be able to buy one if you live in one […]
content: Tesla is doubling, or perhaps tripling down on its bold claims of an autonomous future with the offer to “select customers” to purchase a Cybercab for “personal use.” But the gilded, steering-wheel-free two-seater will “only be available in supported service areas” — meaning you’ll only be able to buy one if you live in one of the cities where Tesla currently operates its Robotaxi service. The price of a Cybercab is listed at $29,990, plus a mandatory $299-a-month “Autonomy Subscription.” Tesla’s Robotaxi account on X announced the new offer, including screenshots of the order page and the invite email. But don’t expect a fleet of personally owned Cybercabs to suddenly materialize on public roads: “Initial availability is limited,” the invitation email warns. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/HXCrorcbwAAQTq0_569a68.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/HXCr4I4bYAA8lrS.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/HXCr4Iza4AErLOW.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Tesla began offering rides in the Cybercab as part of its Model Y-powered Robotaxi service in Austin in September. The company now has 278 Cybercabs in operation, representing approximately 40 percent of its fleet, according to the crowd-sourced Robotaxi Tracker. The inclusion of a mandatory $299/month subscription is sure to rankle some fans who may have dreamed of cruising around in a $30,000 driverless Tesla, as originally promised by Tesla CEO Elon Musk when he first introduced the Cybercab in 2024. Musk made no mention of the Autonomy Subscription at that event, though it shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise given the $99/month fee Tesla currently charges for its Full Self-Driving (FSD) feature. Still, that money adds up over time. Over a standard 5-year ownership period, the mandatory $299/month fee adds $17,940 to the sticker price (even with the first month included), bringing the real baseline cost to roughly $47,600 before taxes, charging, and insurance — more than a brand-new Model 3 or Model Y that you can actually drive anywhere in the country. Unlike a standard Tesla where canceling FSD just reverts the car to manual driving, canceling the $299/month Autonomy Subscription renders the Cybercab completely unusable on public roads because there is no manual fallback. In effect, the car becomes a brick. Additionally, Tesla says that buyers will have to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit just to get in line for a December delivery window that isn’t guaranteed. One of the biggest selling points of Musk’s 2024 “We, Robot” pitch was that regular people could buy a Cybercab and add it to Tesla’s Robotaxi network to earn passive income while they sleep or work. But the order terms explicitly prohibit owners from using the vehicle for commercial purposes — meaning no Uber, no DoorDash, and no putting it on Tesla’s own Robotaxi network to offset the $299/month fee. Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy has floated Q2 2027 as a possible target for letting customer cars join the network, so early buyers are paying full freight with zero way to monetize the car. Moreover, Tesla only has to give you 30 days’ warning before raising the price. If they update the rules and you keep using the service, you automatically agree to the new terms. Also, if you cancel — or if Tesla suspends your access — you won’t get a partial refund for the rest of the month you already paid for. Of course, that’s just the fine print. On X, Tesla CEO Elon Musk was promising a much wider rollout, subject — of course — to “regulatory approval.” Musk frequently frames regulatory approval as the primary external bottleneck holding back his robotaxi timelines as a way to shift focus away from Tesla’s technological shortcomings. (For what it’s worth, he also called his own company’s $299/month Autonomy Subscription “too high,” arguing that it should actually be $115/month or closer to Tesla’s $99/month Full Self-Driving subscription.) But Musk seemed more focused on taunting YouTuber Marques Brownlee, who promised to shave his head if Tesla delivered a Cybercab for under $30,000 before 2027, than answering any of the litany of safety and liability questions raised by this offer. (For his part, Brownlee says he thinks his hair is safe.) For starters, how does Tesla plan on selling a vehicle that doesn’t comply with current Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards that require traditional controls like steering wheels and pedals? Tesla says the Autonomy Subscription covers autonomous driving, maintenance, and towing, but explicitly excludes auto insurance. The company hasn’t explained how personal auto insurers will underwrite a car with no human driver, or how liability is split between the owner and Tesla if the vehicle causes an accident while operating autonomously. Nor has Tesla disclosed how it selects invited buyers or how many units are earmarked for private sale versus its internal fleet. Then there is the small matter of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration already opening a formal audit into how Tesla self-certified a vehicle without a steering wheel, pedals, or side mirrors. Tesla submitted its legal justification to NHTSA in October, requested that the entire response be kept confidential, and is now taking customer deposits while NHTSA’s ruling is still pending. Which means early buyers aren’t just paying $47,600 for a geofenced car they aren’t allowed to drive — they’re putting down non-refundable cash on a vehicle the federal government hasn’t even decided is street-legal.
chineseTitle: 特斯拉邀请一些人购买“供个人使用”的 Cyber​​cab，但请阅读细则
chineseSummary: 特斯拉正在加倍甚至三倍地兑现其对自动驾驶未来的大胆主张，向“精选客户”提供购买 Cyber​​cab 供“个人使用”的优惠。但这款镀金、无方向盘的两座车将“仅在支持的服务区域提供”——这意味着如果您住在一个[…]
chineseContent: 特斯拉正在加倍甚至三倍地兑现其对自动驾驶未来的大胆主张，向“精选客户”提供购买 Cyber​​cab 供“个人使用”的优惠。但这款镀金、无方向盘的两座车将“仅在受支持的服务区域提供”——这意味着如果你住在特斯拉目前运营其 Robotaxi 服务的城市之一，你就只能购买一辆。 Cyber​​cab 的标价为 29,990 美元，另加每月 299 美元的强制性“Autonomy 订阅”。特斯拉 X 上的 Robotaxi 帐户宣布了新优惠，包括订单页面的屏幕截图和邀请电子邮件。但不要指望私人拥有的网络出租车车队会突然出现在公共道路上：邀请电子邮件警告说，“最初的可用性有限”。 [图片：https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/HXCrorcbwAAQTq0_569a68.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [图片： https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/HXCr4I4bYAA8lrS.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [图片： https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/HXCr4Iza4AErLOW.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] 9 月份，特斯拉开始在奥斯汀提供 Cybercab 乘车服务，作为其 Model Y 驱动的 Robotaxi 服务的一部分。根据众包的 Robotaxi Tracker 数据，该公司目前有 278 辆 Cyber​​taxi 正在运营，约占其车队的 40%。包含每月 299 美元的强制性订阅肯定会激怒一些粉丝，他们可能梦想着乘坐价值 30,000 美元的无人驾驶特斯拉到处兜风，正如特斯拉首席执行官埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 在 2024 年首次推出 Cyber​​cab 时所承诺的那样。马斯克在那次活动中没有提及 Autonomy 订阅，不过考虑到特斯拉目前收取的每月 99 美元的费用，这并不令人意外。
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于 AI 与科技趋势信号，适合用于观察工具选型、产品机会、开发者关注点和技术路线变化。
